title: What If You Actually Lived in a Cyberpunk City?
analysis_notes: Downloaded on the Spark at 854x480 30fps (format 397 + opus 251 merged to AAC, 32 MB, kept since <300 MB) to ~/studio/refs/whatif/vibKA0QbtMg.mp4 with info.json, webp thumbnail and en/en-orig auto-subs (word-timed, about 1,560 spoken words). Metadata at about 09:30 UTC: 149,535 views, 1,843 likes (1.23% like rate, higher than the channel's outlier J3XahLkDEzU at 0.45%), 76 comments, 19k subs, posted 2026-10-10 (3 weeks old). It sits exactly at the channel median, so it is the CONTROL for the same channel's 6.1x outlier 'What If You Were the Last Human on Earth?' (J3XahLkDEzU): same hero (spiky hair, brass goggles, teal jacket, yellow satchel), same narrator voice, same 2.5D flat-shaded ink-outline style, same second-person present tense. YouTube chapters: 0:00 Life on the ground floor, 1:23 The courier's assignment, 2:40 Ascending the city levels, 4:02 The world of augmented reality, 5:47 Inside the corporate zone, 7:06 Reaching the canopy, 8:32 The cost of a blue sky. Category Film & Animation; 15 tags ('cyberpunk', 'cyberpunk city', 'living in a cyberpunk world', 'futuristic city', 'dystopian future', 'sci fi animation'...). Frames sampled every 2 s (294) -> contact sheet sheets/vibKA0QbtMg.jpg (15x20 grid of 106x60 tiles; tile n, 0-indexed row-major = t 2n s). Scene detection (ffmpeg scene>0.25) found 163 cuts. Full timestamped transcript at research/library/transcripts/vibKA0QbtMg.txt. Audio mean -17.9 dB, peak -0.7 dB; 9 music-only holds of 2.5-7 s. Structure: a single-delivery quest ('take a package from Level 1 to Level 300') used as an elevator ride through a vertical class system, one level-band per chapter, with a setup/payoff twist (the ground floor's sky is a painted ceiling; the package is the paint). Why it is likely only median vs the outlier: the premise 'cyberpunk city' is a genre label, not a gut-level personal scenario ('last human on Earth' is primal and highly searched); the title promises a genre tour, the thumbnail promises a twist ('THE SKY IS FAKE') that the title does not, so title and thumbnail tell two different stories; and the hook (tiny flat logistics) is witty but low-stakes, with no threat or loss in the first 30 s. Don't reuse its world (Tessera), jokes, characters or wording.
title_pattern: 'What If You Actually Lived in a Cyberpunk City?' = [What If] + [You] + [Actually] + [lived in a fictional/genre setting]. 'Actually' signals 'realistic, mundane detail of a fantasy', which is the channel's real promise (the everyday logistics of a sci-fi place). 47 characters, no number. Weaker than the outlier title because 'cyberpunk city' is an aesthetic category rather than a situation with stakes; it pulls genre fans (search tags 'cyberpunk', 'futuristic city') rather than everyone. The thumbnail carries a separate, stronger hook ('THE SKY IS FAKE') that the title doesn't echo.

thumbnail.source: Custom 1280x720 thumbnail drawn with the video's assets (ground-floor skyline from 0:46, hero bust), not a frame grab.
thumbnail.composition: Text block top-left over two lines: 'THE SKY' in huge white bold sans with a black outline, then 'IS' white and 'FAKE' in black on a slightly tilted yellow rounded box. A thick red curved arrow sweeps from the yellow box up to a white sun disc top-centre-right that is circled by a thick yellow ring. The hero's head and shoulders (bulging eyes, open grin, goggles on forehead, teal jacket, yellow satchel strap) are cropped in at the bottom-right, looking at the camera. Background: a softened, slightly blurred blue-grey skyline of stacked boxy towers with pale clouds.
thumbnail.text: THE SKY IS FAKE (3 words + 'IS'; 'FAKE' boxed)
thumbnail.colours: Muted blue-grey/teal background (sky #8FB3C6-ish, towers grey-brown), white text with black stroke, saturated yellow (#F5C842-ish) box and ring, saturated red arrow (#D8282A-ish). The three saturated accents are the only high-chroma elements, so the eye goes text -> arrow -> sun -> face.
thumbnail.subject_scale_contrast: Big text (about 45% of the frame) vs a small sun target (about 10%) that the arrow points at, plus a mid-sized face. The 'circle and arrow' points at an ordinary object and claims it is fake: classic curiosity-gap thumbnail grammar.
thumbnail.why_it_works: It makes one concrete, checkable, surprising claim (the sky is fake) with a visual pointer to the exact thing, and the hero's delighted face sets a playful, not scary, tone. It sells the video's twist, not its genre. Weaknesses: it doesn't say 'cyberpunk' or show neon, so it is disconnected from the title; the busy text-arrow-circle combo looks like generic clickbait next to the outlier's clean before/after split, and the background is low-contrast and blurred, so at small sizes the scene doesn't read.

hook.verbatim_0_to_5s: (0-3.5 s: no voice; black screen with a pink HUD label typing '1.2 m2 · CITY VIEW', cut at 2.2 s to the hero's face squashed in a tiny window.) Your flat is 1.2 square meters,
hook.verbatim_5_to_30s: so mornings are mostly logistics. The bed folds into the shower, which is also the wardrobe, which is also technically the kitchen. Breakfast prints out of the wall while you're still rinsing. Rent is paid in attention. Ads play in the corner of your eye, and every second you spend watching one knocks a little off the bill. This month you're trying a new strategy, not looking. It lasts about 4 seconds. Your wrist buzzes. A job offer for level 300.
hook.device: Cold open on an absurd-but-specific number ('1.2 square meters') in second person, present tense, then a 'rule of three that escalates' joke (shower = wardrobe = technically kitchen) and two world rules stated as everyday facts ('Breakfast prints out of the wall', 'Rent is paid in attention'), each shown at the same time with a HUD element (ad popup, a rent counter ticking down). A deflating time joke ('It lasts about 4 seconds') is later called back in the climax ('It takes about 4 seconds'). The inciting call (a Level 300 job) lands at 0:31, and the world name and premise ('Tessera, 300 levels stacked on top of each other') are held back to 0:51 as a title reveal with a music hold. The phrase 'It's always a nice day' at 0:49 secretly plants the fake-sky twist.
hook.visual: One continuous animated set for 0:02-0:17 (no detected cut): the camera reframes from the face in a window to a top-down bed that rotates upright into a shower and then into a standing pose, so the tiny flat is explained by transformation rather than by cuts. HUD overlays in pink/magenta (ad card top-left, rent counter bottom-right ticking 411.55 -> 408.05) are the 'cyberpunk' signal.
hook.weakness_vs_outlier: Stakes in the first 30 s are comic (rent, ads), not existential; the 'what if' scenario isn't stated until 0:51, and the hook explains a world rather than showing a loss or mystery.

beats.summary: No intro. 'Your flat is 1.2 square meters' over a face squashed in a tiny window; the bed folds into the shower/wardrobe/'technically the kitchen' as the set transforms.

Breakfast prints from the wall; 'Rent is paid in attention': ads in the corner of your eye knock money off the bill (HUD counter ticks down). Joke: you try not looking, it lasts about 4 seconds (planted for the climax).
Wrist buzzes: a job offer for Level 300. Nobody from down here gets those, so it's a typo or a scam; you swipe it away. Quick-cut 'boots, bag, goggles' kit-up montage.

Door opens to the street: 'It's a nice day. It's always a nice day' (plants the fake sky). 'This is Tessera, 300 levels stacked on top of each other' with a big faded title on the sky, then one unbroken vertical pan up the whole stack (slums -> greener floors -> canopy), zoom back out, music hold, 'You live on the ground floor.'

Machines do most jobs (drive, cook, file, diagnose, birthday cards joke) shown as a pen plotter crossing out job titles until 'COURIER (HUMAN)'. Having a job at all is unusual; people look impressed, then worried.

Drones handle deliveries; you get the ones they can't: narrow stairwells, nowhere to land, customers who want a person. Three quick customer types (a pulse signature, an unrecorded delivery, 'some just like being handed things', planted for 8:41). Paid per job and rated after every one.
Real sunlight is piped down by fiber-optic cable and sold by the minute like water; the Sunday queue goes around the block (sets up the sky theme).

What the ground floor has that upstairs doesn't: vat-grown food that's the best in the city; nothing thrown away, anything broken gets fixed (phones, drones, implants, knees), 'usually him': a 30-year repairman with no implants who made your goggles, which block the overlay (plant).

The Level 300 job comes back with a higher fee, a week's rent. You've never been above Level 40. Locker pickup: small, sealed, heavier than it looks, no sender. '300 floors. You're going to need the tram.' Music hold.

Trams run up the inside of the city every 90 s, silent; pay by floor. First-timer mistake: get off one floor early and take the stairs, built by a fitness company, 40 minutes, smoothie bar halfway. 'You don't make that mistake twice.' (callback at 9:19).

Level-by-level tour while riding up: drone lanes in coloured stripes, express pods that skip districts, Level 60 vertical farms under purple light, Level 88 beach (real sand, the sea is a big screen and a fan), Level 100 reverse commute. 'Level 120, the doors open.'

Glitch-typed 'OVERLAY' title card. Level 120 AR district: marble walls, moss floors, every window a different century, clothes are software (buy a grey jumpsuit, subscribe to how it looks), floating name tags, live translation, a wall turned into an ocean, concerts inside your eyes (10,000 people silent in a square).

You get distracted: a free-trial suit over your hoodie; lunch is the same beige cube everywhere but today it's lasagna. Goggles down mid-bite: marble = concrete, moss = printed carpet, the restaurant is a vending machine, the crowd wears grey jumpsuits. 'Everybody knows, they just prefer the other version. So do you.'
Ratings float over heads; yours is 3.9 and you don't know why; your landlord and bank can see it. Cliffhanger: every overlay in the street turns red at once (music hold).

Level 200, the company floors. The checkpoint knows your name, rating, heart rate, breakfast and last search ('how far up is the sky?', plant). Reads you as 'suspiciously hopeful' and your suit as executive; the free trial ends mid-scan; the box has higher clearance than you, so it is let through and you go with it.

Quiet, clean, people live where they work (beds fold out of desks), bonuses paid in sunlight minutes; the company is landlord, doctor and from Level 240 your kids' school; a department asleep at the same time, 'It's in the calendar'. Public lifts stop at 280; 'nobody checks the service lift'.

A layer nobody visits on purpose: where the air goes (cutaway diagram: the top breathes out, vents carry it down, 'Filtered, mostly'). Goggles down, nothing changes; nobody decorated it. A crew mixes sky blue and cloud white paint in huge drums 'for the ceiling you woke up under this morning': the ground floor's sky is painted. 'Somebody upstairs picks the colors.'
An unlocked hatch, a ladder, and the real sky: 'bigger than you expected, and it moves.' Long music hold. 'You stay a while. Nobody bills you for it.' (pays off sunlight-by-the-minute).

'THE CANOPY' gate. Real trees and birds with a waiting list for both; residents complain when it's cloudy; quiet, slow, never go downstairs, have seen it in documentaries; no ads, 'that's what they're paying for'. The address is a glass pavilion where the facilities committee meets on sun loungers. 'This is why they asked for a person. They like being handed things.' (callback).

They open the box: a tin of paint labelled 'Sky, ground level, proposed'. A stripe held against the real sky: too bright, unrealistic. The only decision about the ground floor they'll make all year takes about 4 seconds (callback); they pick a grey, 'Overcast Premium', cheaper and 'hard to tell the difference'. Five stars; they ask you to throw the blue away. 'You don't.'
Stairs one floor on principle (callback). A week later the painters turn the ground-floor sky grey by lunchtime. 'It looks fine. People adjust. They usually do.'

Except above one repair stall (the mentor's), a small square of blue nobody approved, the size of a window. Final joke closes the loop on rent/attention/sunlight economics: 'Rent on that spot has already gone up.' No CTA, end card.

pacing.words_per_minute_while_speaking: about 170-172 (about 40 s of music-only holds and the 3.5 s silent open removed)
pacing.wpm_by_section: 0-60 s: 137; 60-120 s: 169; 120-240 s: 174; 240-360 s: 155; 360-480 s: 152; 480-587 s: 148. Fastest in the explainer middle, slowing into the twist and ending.
pacing.music_only_holds: 9 holds of 2.5-7 s: 0:43 (door opens, about 5 s), 0:56 (Tessera title, about 7 s), 2:50 (tram), 3:59 (doors open), 5:43 (overlays turn red), 7:01 (service lift), 7:46, 7:54-8:00 (real sky, about 6 s), 8:02
pacing.shot_length_range: 0.7-2 s for kit-up and list inserts; 3-6 s typical; long unbroken 12-16 s shots for the transforming flat (0:02-0:17) and the vertical pan over the whole city (0:51-1:07)
pacing.chapter_cards: 7 YouTube chapters about every 80 s; in-video markers are level numbers spoken as headers ('Level 60', 'Level 88', 'Level 120', 'Level 200', 'Level 300') plus two typed title cards (TESSERA, OVERLAY) and a stone gate (THE CANOPY)
pacing.rehook_interval_s: about 25-40 s: each level opens with a new wonder or rule and ends on a deflating joke; bigger cliffhangers at 5:40 (every overlay turns red) and 7:00 (nobody checks the service lift)
pacing.notes: Rhythm per section: '[Level N]' header -> 2-4 world rules stated as everyday facts -> list of three -> dry deflating joke. Jokes land about every 15-20 s, more often than the outlier, but there is less emotional weight until the 7:44 real-sky moment. Narration is calm, British-leaning and dry, never shouted.

techniques_worth_copying: Quest-as-tour spine: one simple errand (deliver a box from the bottom to the top) turns a world explainer into a story with a destination; each chapter is one stop on the route, so progress is obvious (level numbers rise).

Vertical-world layering as a class map: altitude = wealth. Each level band gets its own palette (brown/amber ground floor, purple farms, pink/gold AR arcade, white/grey corporate, near-black service layer, bright green/blue canopy) so the viewer feels the climb by colour alone.

Plant-and-payoff density: 'It's always a nice day' (0:49) -> painted sky (7:38); 'some just like being handed things' (1:42) -> 'This is why they asked for a person' (8:39); 'It lasts about 4 seconds' (0:28) -> 'It takes about 4 seconds' (9:02); stairs mistake (3:07) -> 'one floor, on principle' (9:19); sunlight sold by the minute (1:50) -> 'Nobody bills you for it' (8:01); goggles block the overlay (2:22) -> reality toggles (5:05, 7:25); repairman (2:11) -> blue square above his stall (9:33). At least 7 callbacks in under 10 minutes.

Mystery object as the engine: the package (small, sealed, heavier than it looks, no sender) is carried in almost every shot and opened only at 8:43; its contents re-frame the whole video (it is the sky paint).

A/B reality toggle: lock the framing and cut between the 'overlay' and 'real' versions of the same shot (restaurant vs vending machine, costumes vs grey jumpsuits). Cheap to build in code (same layout, two style sets) and very legible.

Rule of three with an escalating last item ('the shower, which is also the wardrobe, which is also technically the kitchen'; 'phones, drones, implants, knees'; 'your landlord, your doctor, and ... your kids' school').

World rules stated as mundane facts in second person ('Rent is paid in attention', 'Their bonuses are paid in sunlight minutes'), each shown with one HUD element so abstract satire becomes a visible UI.
Diegetic HUD as the genre signal: magenta/pink rounded cards, counters, rating badges and wrist pop-ups do the 'cyberpunk' work instead of expensive neon environments.
Two long unbroken 'world' shots early (transforming flat, continuous crane-up over all 300 levels) give scale and set up every later location before the story visits it.

Bittersweet small-victory ending with a satirical sting ('Rent on that spot has already gone up') instead of a CTA; the last image is a tableau that sums up the theme (a window of blue above the one person who fixes things).

code_only_remake_requirements.assets: One rigged SVG hero (spiky hair, goggles up/down, 3 eye states incl. squeeze-shut and wide, open-grin and neutral mouths, teal jacket, satchel; poses: front stand, back view, walking, holding a box, sitting, climbing hand), a mentor and 8-10 simple background people (stick-limb bodies, varied hair/skin/clothes) with a 'grey jumpsuit' style variant; about 15 SVG sets drawn in flat 2.5D one-point perspective: micro-flat interior (with transforming bed/shower), neon alley, market street with awnings, repair stall, locker bank, tram shaft and pod, vertical farm corridor, screen-beach, AR arcade (2 style versions), checkpoint with scanner arch, white open-plan office, dark vent/fan shaft, roof with real sky, canopy avenue, glass pavilion. Props: box with label, paint tin, swatch fan, drones, pen plotter, split-flap counter, fiber-optic meter. A tall 'whole city stack' illustration (about 1920x8000) for the crane-up shot and a cutaway diagram version.
code_only_remake_requirements.layout: 16:9 1920x1080. Muted, warm-desaturated palette with a soft vignette and light film grain; ink outlines (2-3 px dark brown). HUD layer in magenta/pink (#C2408F-ish) rounded rectangles with a thin glow, small geometric sans (e.g. Space Grotesk/Inter) for labels and counters; title cards in wide-tracked caps on dark purple.
code_only_remake_requirements.camera: Mostly static frames with slow push-ins (scale 1.00 -> 1.06 over 4-8 s); one-point perspective alleys/offices pushed toward the vanishing point; a long vertical pan over a tall image (translateY over 15 s with 3-4 parallax layers); pull-out reveals (the screen-beach, the city stack) via scale interpolation; one whip-pan transition (motion blur via a horizontal CSS blur keyframe). All do-able with Remotion interpolate() on transform.
code_only_remake_requirements.motion: HUD cards pop with a scale overshoot (spring) and a subtle glitch; counters tick (rent, rating 3.9 -> 3.91, fare); a plotter strike-through drawn with strokeDashoffset while the paper list scrolls; split-flap digits flip; glitch-typed title letters; a red tint and warning triangles popping on a stagger; a scan line sweeping down; a blueprint wireframe of the hero drawn with strokes and icons attaching; a set that transforms (bed rotating into shower) via rotate/translate on grouped SVG parts; cloud drift and slow sun glow; simple 2-frame limb swings for walking; eye blinks.
code_only_remake_requirements.audio_and_captions: Calm, dry second-person narration at about 160-170 wpm (Kokoro/Piper on CPU), a soft synth/lo-fi music bed with 3-7 s music-only holds at reveals; no burned-in captions in the reference (on-screen text is diegetic only). Light SFX: wrist buzz, door, tram hum, scanner beep.
code_only_remake_requirements.hard_parts: Volume of bespoke environments (about 15 sets) is the main cost; reuse one perspective-grid generator for alleys/arcade/office/shafts and recolour per level band. The A/B overlay toggle needs each arcade asset in two skins (colour and grey). Keep character acting minimal (the reference does too: mostly stand, look and react).
